name: Raised Back of Hand: Medium-Dark Skin Tone
baseMeaning: The back of a raised hand. The medium-dark skin tone modifier is applied to the hand.
tldr: 🤚🏾 Raised Back of Hand with a medium-dark skin tone. Reached deliberately, so it reads as intentional.

contextMeanings.meaning: Shows the same artwork as the untoned version, with the medium-dark skin tone applied to the hand.
The gesture reads the same as the untoned version; the medium-dark skin tone makes it a chosen version rather than a defaulted one.
In a dating thread the gesture is unchanged; the tone makes it a deliberate statement about who is being pictured.
In a work thread the gesture is unchanged, and the medium-dark skin tone still reads as intentional, but without the extra weight the darkest tone carries.

platformNotes.note: On iOS 🤚🏾 renders as a single toned glyph, and the medium-dark swatch is the fourth of the five in Apple's picker — it takes an extra tap past the three before it. Because it is chosen less often, it is also the one a sender is most likely to have picked on purpose.

WhatsApp lists the medium-dark swatch fourth and renders it correctly on current builds, but older Android versions of the app fall back to the untoned glyph. In practice the medium-dark variant is one of the tones that loses its meaning most often in forwarded messages, because the fallback removes the part that was deliberate.

Twemoji applies the tone to 🤚🏾 consistently. The medium-dark swatch holds its contrast better on a white background than the darkest one does, so it survives screenshotting and re-posting more often than the tone it sits next to.

Slack's emoji font renders the medium-dark swatch with less contrast than the phone version does, and the difference is more noticeable here than for the lighter tones. People who picked the swatch to represent themselves can look under-represented in a Slack screenshot for no reason other than the font.

Discord uses Twemoji, so the modifier is preserved, but bots and integrations that rewrite messages are the weak point. The medium-dark swatch is the one most likely to arrive untoned, and the reason it was chosen in the first place is usually the reason it matters.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reads 🤚🏾 as a deliberate choice, because the swatch takes extra taps to reach. This cohort is also the most likely to notice when 🤚🏾 has been used to depict somebody else, and to read that as a statement about the person.

Millennials pick 🤚🏾 when representing themselves, and treat it as personal in a way they do not treat the lighter tones. It is also the tone most often borrowed to depict somebody else in this cohort.
Gen X is less likely to change the tone at all, so 🤚🏾 appears mostly in messages where the sender was depicting themselves. The swatch is read as personal rather than political.

warnings.title: Borrowed skin tones are the usual failure point
warnings.description: 🤚🏾 is frequently used to depict somebody other than its sender, and it is the tone most often used to represent a person who is not the sender, which is where the misreading starts. When the person being depicted is in the room, the tone is read as a description of them.

seoTitle: 🤚🏾 Raised Back of Hand Medium-Dark Skin Tone Emoji Meaning - What Does 🤚🏾 Mean?
seoDescription: What does the raised back of hand emoji 🤚🏾 mean? Raised Back of Hand showing a hand held up with the back of it turned toward the reader, the knuckles showing. Covers the medium-dark skin tone variant, the misread it invites, and how to reply.

longForm.overview:
🤚🏾 is Raised Back of Hand with a medium-dark skin tone — a hand held up with the back of it turned toward the reader, the knuckles showing. The gesture is the familiar one, doing what it always does: showing empty hands, or waving without the warmth of a palm-forward wave. What makes this variant worth its own page is that the tone is not an accident. It is the fourth swatch in the tone list, which means it takes an extra tap past the three before it, and that effort shows up in how the message lands.

The upshot is that 🤚🏾 reads as chosen. Where a first-swatch emoji can be waved past, a tone someone had to reach for tends to be read as a small, deliberate piece of information — usually about who the message is coming from, occasionally about who it is about. Neither reading is wrong, but they are not interchangeable, and that is where the confusion with ✋ Raised Hand comes from: the palm-forward raised hand reads as a greeting or a high five, the turned one reads as hands-up or a sign-off.

The situations it turns up in are the family ones, unchanged by the tone. The misread that keeps coming up is this: it gets taken for the palm-forward raised hand because the two sit next to each other in every picker, so a hands-up gesture arrives as a greeting and a sign-off arrives as a high five.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
The gesture is the same one 🤚 makes, so the family habits carry straight over. What changes with 🤚🏾 is who tends to send it and what they are assuming about the reader.

Medium-dark takes an extra tap to reach, and 🤚🏾 shows up in the places where that extra tap was made on purpose: profile photos, avatars, introductions, and the emoji people pick for themselves rather than for a situation. It appears in answering an accusation with a clean pair of hands, and in signing off from a thread you are done with, and it is more likely than the other tones to be the sender's own.

It is also the tone that gets borrowed most, because it sits closer to the middle of the list and so reads as a reasonable approximation of a lot of people. When 🤚🏾 is used to stand in for somebody else, the tone is quietly doing a job the sender never mentioned.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
The family rule applies first, and it is the one spelled out above: the standard misread of this glyph belongs to 🤚 itself, and every tone in this family inherits it.

The tone-specific rule for 🤚🏾 is about borrowed representation. This is the swatch people reach for when they are depicting somebody else, and it is the swatch most likely to be wrong. If you are sending 🤚🏾 to stand in for another person, either know that you are doing it deliberately and accept that it will read that way, or use 🤚 instead.

Also avoid 🤚🏾 in professional threads where a chosen skin tone on a neutral emoji can look like a stance the message never made. The tone says the sender chose it, and readers will read the choice even when the sentence does not support it.
longForm.howToReply:
Matching the swatch is the acknowledging move here. If somebody picks a tone deliberately and you reply with 🏾, you are telling them you noticed; 🤚 reads as though you did not.

Keep the reply proportionate otherwise. A sentence that names the moment will land better than a mirrored emoji when the message is the kind that invites a reply — the gesture is a good conversation opener on its own.

faqs.question: What does 🤚🏾 mean in chat?
faqs.answer: 🤚🏾 is Raised Back of Hand with a medium-dark skin tone. The gesture reads as showing empty hands, or waving without the warmth of a palm-forward wave, and the tone reads as chosen rather than defaulted to.

faqs.question: Why does 🤚🏾 feel more intentional than 🤚?
faqs.answer: Because of the picker position. It is the fourth swatch in the tone list, which means it takes an extra tap past the three before it. A swatch that takes extra taps gets read as a decision.

faqs.question: What does 🤚🏾 mean from a girl?
faqs.answer: The gesture reads the same as it does from anyone else. The tone does not add a gendered layer to 🤚.

faqs.question: Is it rude to use 🤚🏾 to describe someone else?
faqs.answer: It can be, and this is the tone where that happens most often. It is the tone most often used to represent a person who is not the sender, which is where the misreading starts. If you are unsure, 🤚 avoids the problem entirely.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🤚🏾 and ✋ Raised Hand?
faqs.answer: the palm-forward raised hand reads as a greeting or a high five, the turned one reads as hands-up or a sign-off.
